chapters.title: Chapter 4: Building and Reading the Volatility Surface

lessons.title: IV Percentile and IV Rank: Putting Today's Surface in Context

children.text: Two Ways to Ask "Is IV High Right Now?"

Every lesson so far has described the shape of IV at a single moment, across strikes, across expiries. This lesson adds a different kind of time dimension: not the future expiries of the term structure, but IV's own recent history, to answer a genuinely different question. Is today's 15% ATM IV actually high, or actually low, compared to how this exact underlying has traded over the last year? Two metrics try to answer that, and they do not always agree.
IV Rank: Where Today Sits Between the Extremes

body.caption: This places today's IV on a 0 to 100 scale, anchored only by the single highest and single lowest IV readings over the lookback window, commonly the trailing 252 trading days.

children.text: IV Percentile: Where Today Sits in the Whole Distribution

IV Percentile asks a related but structurally different question: out of every trading day in the same lookback window, what percentage had an IV lower than today's? A reading of 85% means today's IV was higher than 85% of all the days in that window, using every single data point, not just the two most extreme ones.

body.text: IV Rank is anchored by exactly two data points: the single highest day and the single lowest day. IV Percentile is built from every day in the window. That structural difference, two points versus the whole distribution, is why the two metrics can tell you completely different stories from the exact same underlying data.

children.text: Why They Can Tell Wildly Different Stories: A Worked Example

body.caption: Illustrative one-year Nifty ATM IV history

cells: Days in the past year with IV below today's 15%

children.text: IV Rank works out to (15 minus 9) divided by (71 minus 9), times 100, which is 6 divided by 62, about 9.7%. On its own, that number screams "IV is near its lowest point of the year." IV Percentile, computed from the same year of data, comes out very differently: 214 of 252 days had IV below today's 15%, which is roughly 84.9%.

stats.label: IV Rank (today)
stats.context: Suggests IV is near its lowest point of the past year

stats.label: IV Percentile (today)
stats.context: Suggests IV is higher than on 85% of the past year's trading days

children.text: Same underlying, same day, same lookback window, two numbers that point in opposite directions. The single 71% crisis day stretched the denominator of the Rank formula so far upward that almost everything else in a normal year gets squashed toward the bottom of that range, even a reading that was genuinely elevated relative to most ordinary trading days. Percentile does not have this problem, because it counts days rather than measuring distance from an extreme.
Using Them: A Timing Filter, Not a Standalone Signal

Traders commonly use IV Rank or IV Percentile as a threshold filter for strategy selection: leaning toward selling premium, like the strategies discussed in Chapter 2's trading lesson, when the reading sits high, and leaning toward buying premium when it sits low. That is a genuinely useful timing habit, but neither metric explains why today's IV sits where it does, and neither says anything at all about the shape covered in the rest of this course, the skew, the term structure, or how steep either currently is. They describe one ATM number's position in its own history, nothing more. The standard lookback window is 252 trading days, roughly a year, but platforms vary, and switching to a 30-day or 90-day window can shift both readings meaningfully on the same underlying.

body.title: Explaining a Rank vs Percentile divergence
body.question: A stock's IV Rank today is a low 12%, but its IV Percentile, using the same one-year lookback window, is a high 88%. What is the most likely explanation for this divergence?
options: This combination is impossible; one of the two numbers must be a calculation error

The stock's 52-week high was likely set by one or a few extreme outlier days, such as a crisis or a major surprise event, which pulled the range's ceiling far above where IV normally trades, compressing today's reading toward the bottom of that wide range even though today's IV is actually higher than most of the year's typical days
IV Rank and IV Percentile always move together, so this could never happen with real data
IV Percentile is simply IV Rank calculated over a shorter lookback window
body.explanation: IV Rank is entirely anchored by the single highest and single lowest readings in the window. One extreme outlier day is enough to stretch that range so far that an otherwise genuinely elevated IV reading gets compressed toward the bottom of it, exactly the pattern this lesson's worked example showed.

body.title: Rethinking a 'low IV Rank' decision
body.scenario: A trader wants to sell a Nifty iron condor only when IV looks rich by historical standards. He checks IV Rank on his broker app, sees a low 10%, and decides today is a bad day to sell premium, planning to wait for a higher reading before entering.
body.prompt: Given this lesson's worked example, what might he be missing, and what should he check before deciding?
body.modelAnswer: He may be missing that IV Percentile could tell a very different, more accurate story if the 52-week high was set by a single rare extreme event day, exactly as in this lesson's worked example. Before concluding IV is genuinely low, he should check IV Percentile alongside IV Rank, and ideally glance at the actual IV history rather than trusting either single number blindly. If Percentile shows something like 85%, today's IV is actually elevated relative to most of the past year, and selling premium could be a reasonable, well-timed decision, the opposite conclusion from what IV Rank alone suggested.

columns.label: IV Rank
points: Uses only two data points: the 52-week high and the 52-week low
Measures where today sits within that extreme-to-extreme range
Highly sensitive to a single outlier day setting the high or low
Simple and widely available on most broker platforms

columns.label: IV Percentile
points: Uses every day in the lookback window
Measures what percentage of days had a lower IV than today
Far more robust to a single outlier day distorting the reading
Arguably the more reliable of the two, though somewhat less universally available

body.text: IV Rank asks how far today sits from the two most extreme days in the past year. IV Percentile asks how today compares to every single one of those days. A market that had one legitimately terrifying day and two hundred and fifty-one ordinary ones can make those two questions return wildly different answers, and only one of them is actually describing what a typical trading day just looked like.

points: IV Rank equals (Today's IV minus 52-week Low) divided by (52-week High minus 52-week Low), times 100, measuring today's position within the extreme-to-extreme range.
IV Percentile equals the percentage of days in the lookback window with IV below today's reading, measuring today's position within the whole historical distribution.

A single extreme outlier day can drag IV Rank down artificially for the rest of the lookback window by stretching the range's ceiling, while IV Percentile stays comparatively robust to that same outlier.

Both metrics are historical-context tools for timing decisions, such as when to favor selling versus buying premium; neither explains why IV is where it is, and neither describes the shape of the skew or term structure.
The standard lookback window is 252 trading days, roughly a year, but platforms vary, and the choice of window can itself change both readings meaningfully.
